ddx.step1_summary:
• Chief complaint: Progressive shortness of breath.
• Symptoms: Dyspnea gradually worsening over 2 weeks, noticeably worse in last few days; now breathless walking to shops and around house. Mild dry cough. Bilateral ankle swelling appearing over last few days. No chest pain, palpitations, fever, or orthostatic symptoms. Feels a little run-down.
• Past medical history: Chronic heart failure (etiology likely ischemic). Remote “small heart attack” ≈5 years ago (probable myocardial infarction). No other chronic illnesses reported.
• Medications: Furosemide (loop diuretic, 1 tab daily—dose unknown); Aspirin; Bisoprolol.  No known drug allergies.
• Family history: Father died of myocardial infarction in early 60s; mother alive with osteoporosis.
• Social history: Lives alone with two cats; part-time lorry driver; ex-smoker (≈25 pack-years, quit); denies alcohol; minimal exercise.
• Vital signs / exam: Exact numbers not provided; clinician states chest exam, oxygen saturations, and blood pressure “all OK.” Bilateral ankle oedema noted by patient (extent not quantified).
• Labs / imaging: None performed yet; plan for blood tests (CBC, renal function) and echocardiogram.

V: Acute decompensated congestive heart failure (ischemic cardiomyopathy): known HF with new volume overload → dyspnea + peripheral oedema.
Acute coronary syndrome / reinfarction precipitating HF flare: prior MI, risk factors, could cause new pump failure and SOB.
I: Viral or bacterial lower-respiratory infection precipitating dyspnea ± HF decompensation: subacute worsening, dry cough.
N: Primary lung malignancy causing progressive dyspnea and cough, though time-course short.
D: COPD exacerbation/development in ex-smoker leading to dyspnea (less likely given no wheeze).
Anemia (iron/B12 deficiency) causing exertional dyspnea and fatigue.
I2: Medication-induced fluid retention (e.g., recent NSAID use) worsening HF; not reported but possible.
C: Congenital valvular or cardiomyopathic lesion with progression—already manifests as HF.
A: Asthma (allergic) presenting with breathlessness—no wheeze, less likely.
T: Pulmonary embolism after prolonged sitting in lorry driving → acute dyspnea, can cause leg swelling if right-heart strain.
E: Hypothyroidism causing fluid retention and fatigue; could exacerbate HF.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Known history of HF with classic symptoms of volume overload (progressive exertional dyspnea, new bilateral ankle oedema). Course and triggers consistent with HF flare.
supporting_evidence: Progressive dyspnea over weeks, markedly worse past few days
Bilateral ankle swelling—common sign of right-sided fluid overload
Exam described as otherwise stable, consistent with compensated but symptomatic HF
opposing_evidence: No reported orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Vital signs reportedly normal (though values unknown)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Lower-respiratory tract infection (viral bronchitis or early pneumonia) precipitating or mimicking dyspnea
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Subacute onset, dry cough, feeling run-down; infections commonly trigger HF exacerbations.
supporting_evidence: New dry cough concurrent with worsening breathlessness
opposing_evidence: No sputum production or pleuritic chest pain

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute worsening breathlessness can reflect PE; lorry-driver sedentary work and prior cardiac disease are risk factors.
supporting_evidence: Sudden subjective worsening over last few days
Sedentary occupation (long drives) could lead to venous stasis
opposing_evidence: Progression described over weeks rather than abrupt hours
No pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, tachycardia, or unilateral leg swelling
Ankle swelling bilateral and likely chronic

supporting_evidence: Complaints of breathlessness and feeling run-down
